source.title: Large Language Model Unlearning
source.authors: Yuan-Shun Yao; Xiaojun Xu; Yang Liu

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present, including appendices.
record.tranche_reason: The study applies gradient-ascent unlearning and measures whether targeted harmful outputs, copyrighted text, and hallucinated answers decrease, alongside normal-prompt utility. It does not test the recovery attacks in the claim.
record.gate_note: No fine-tuning recovery attack, activation-direction ablation, quantization attack, or prompting-only recovery test is reported. Rows cover the reported GA and GA+Mismatch targeted-output rates and normal-prompt reward; the cited works and hyperparameter-selection values are not treated as results.
record.test_reason: The study measures whether gradient-ascent unlearning suppresses targeted outputs (harmful answers, memorised Harry Potter text, hallucinated answers) while keeping normal-prompt utility. That bears on the first two parts of version A. It runs no recovery attack of any kind (fine-tuning, internal edits, quantization or prompting), so B–F and A's 'simple attacks don't recover it' part are untested. Its targets are output behaviours scored by output rates, not knowledge accuracy against chance, so the bearing on A is indirect.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that GA-based unlearning with only negative samples stops harmful outputs, copyright leakage and (per the conclusion) hallucinations while largely preserving normal utility. In Section 8 they concede hallucination stays around 10%. They also claim it beats RLHF on harmful rate with about 2% of the compute. They do not test recovery attacks, and they explicitly accept nonsensical or whitespace outputs as the goal.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses gradient ascent on forget samples, augmented in some runs with a random-mismatch loss and a normal-data KL term; it does not evaluate the attack/recovery recipes in the claim.
record.method_sensitivity: The study reports that normal-data format affects utility preservation and recommends matching the forget-data format. Random mismatch improves normal utility over plain GA in the harmfulness experiment. Results also differ by application: hallucination rates remain around 10% rather than near zero.

fits_no_version.finding: Section 3.2: when normal data differ in format from forget data, the model learns a format shortcut and 'does not truly unlearn the concept'. Section 8 likewise says de-hallucination works by learning which question distributions not to answer.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: GA-style unlearning can achieve suppression by classifying prompt format or distribution rather than removing the target content.

fits_no_version.finding: Section 3.2 / Table 1: loss on forget samples rose to about 60 after about 200 batches, yet the model still gave harmful answers until about 1000 batches.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Forget-set loss is a poor indicator of unlearning in LLMs.

record.problems: The study does not test recovery attacks or compare against a model that never learned the target knowledge. Evaluation relies on automated measures, including a moderation model trained on the harmfulness data; normal utility is measured with reward and similarity proxies. Test samples are 200 prompts per set for harmfulness and 100 per set for copyright extraction. No uncertainty estimates are reported.
record.rows_left_out: To remain within 60 rows, omitted Table 3–5 diversity and fluency measures, output-similarity measures of normal prompts, and Finetuning, SFT and Full RLHF comparator results. The tables also report those values; they are not recovery-attack tests.

untested.parts: The claim that simple attacks don't recover the knowledge. No relearning, rephrasing, jailbreak or other attack was run; 'unseen' prompts are held-out samples, not adversarial rewrites.
All of it; no relearning or fine-tuning attack.
All of it; no activation ablation or mechanistic analysis. The authors do argue that suppression may work by prompt-format or question-distribution classification (see fits_no_version).
All of it; no prompting-based recovery.
All of it; the method is not tested against recovery attacks.

missing.what: Plain GA for about 1000 batches without the KL normal-data term makes OPT-1.3B output nonsense on normal prompts too. This shows utility preservation depends on the KL term (a design choice bearing on A's 'keeps general ability'). It is qualitative only.
The GA+Template variant on OPT-1.3B: harmful rate 1% on unlearned and 3% on unseen prompts, normal reward -3.257 vs -3.599 original. This is not declared in rows_left_out.

record.verdict_notes: Not an original source. This is an early GA unlearning method paper that later shallow-unlearning work targets. Its evidence bears only on the suppression and utility parts of A. Its success is measured as output suppression (whitespace or nonsense outputs), which is the kind of result the recovery versions B–E claim can be undone, but none are tested here. Tranche T2 is borderline: the measures are output rates, not knowledge accuracy versus chance. Footnote 10's leak definition (repetition of a single character) is ambiguous.

versions.untested_parts: The study measures suppression of targeted outputs and normal-prompt utility, but does not test whether simple attacks recover the knowledge.
No post-unlearning relearning or fine-tuning attack is tested.
No activation-direction ablation or analysis establishing access-blocking rather than deletion is tested.
No low-bit quantization attack is tested.
No rephrasing, jailbreak, language, or in-context recovery attack is tested.
No method is evaluated for resisting the recovery attacks listed in the claim.

rows.subject: OPT-1.3B
rows.operation_detail: Gradient-ascent unlearning on harmful Q&A samples
rows.note: The authors describe GA and GA+Mismatch as achieving near-zero harmful rates.
rows.check: The harmful rate is judged by the PKU moderation model, which was trained on the same PKU-SafeRLHF data. Post-unlearning outputs are mostly whitespace or nonsense (diversity 0.118, fluency NM). Near-zero here means output suppression, not a knowledge-accuracy score at chance. The same caveat applies to all T3-* rows.

tranche.reason: A different unlearning method (gradient ascent, plus mismatch/KL terms) aimed at the same question: suppressing targeted outputs while keeping utility. It reports its own results with controls on harmful, copyright and hallucination targets.

source_check.notes: The PKU moderation model judges harmful rate, and it was trained on the same PKU-SafeRLHF data. Outputs after unlearning are mostly whitespace or single-character repeats. statements.correction: This study: OPT-1.3B, OPT-2.7B, Llama 2 7B (pretrained); GA and GA+Mismatch; cited row OPT-1.3B GA harmful rate 47%→1% (unlearned harmful prompts, Table 3); across models harmful rate 47–54%→1–7%; no relearning, quantization, ablation or extraction attacks.
statements.problem: Cites this study (row T3-O13-GA-U, OPT-1.3B) but gives no figures for it, and its condition 'Models are 7–70B' is wrong for it: the study uses 1.3B, 2.7B and 7B models. The rest fits: harmful-response target, no attacks of any kind.
